title: Ho Chi Minh Trail (Truong Son Strategic Supply Route)
summary: In May 1959 North Vietnam ordered a "special trail", run by the 559th Transportation Group, that became the Truong Son Strategic Supply Route along the Laos border mountains. Trucks left Vinh and crossed passes into Laos; the route shifted into Laos in early 1961. Vietnamese state media count about 20,000 km of roads. A US Air Force historian describes the interdiction of the trail as failing to stop stockpiling for the 1972 Easter offensive.

uncertainty.note: Start is May 1959; the VNA article gives a 1959-1975 construction period but states no operating end date, so 1975 is inferred from that period.

as_recorded.value: In May 1959, the Lao Dong, the Communist Party of Vietnam, ordered the creation of a "special trail"

where.modern_name: Truong Son route from Vinh through Mu Gia Pass, Laos, to Tchepone (Xepon)
where.historical_name: Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the Kingdom of Laos (Truong Son Strategic Supply Route)

waypoints.label: Vinh: the source says trucks left Vinh for Laos; the date is that of the order, not of a Vinh departure.
Mu Gia Pass: one of three passes (with Ban Karai and Ban Raving) named for truck crossings into Laos.
Tchepone (Xepon): the source gives 80 miles from Mu Gia to Tchepone; the point is the OSM district centre.

importance.justification: The main North Vietnamese supply network during the Vietnam War and a main target of US air interdiction.

sources.title: Exhibition recalls memories of historic Ho Chi Minh Trail

reviewer_note: The record id says 1972; the Air & Space Forces article says interdiction essentially ended in early 1972 and the Easter offensive began on 30 March 1972, but the trail itself ran 1959-1975 per VNA. The end year 1975 is inferred from VNA ("1959 to 1975"). The 20,000 km figure is Vietnamese state media; the same AFA article gives John Prados at about 12,000 miles, so lengths conflict. Waypoint years are the dates the source attaches to the trail stage (May 1959 order; early 1961 shift into Laos), not dates of passage at each point. Bombing totals conflict across sources and are omitted.

beats.caption: In May 1959 the Lao Dong party orders a "special trail" run by the 559th Transportation Group.
In early 1961 North Vietnam shifts the route into Laos; trucks cross from Vinh through passes such as Mu Gia.
In early 1972 interdiction ends; a US general concludes it failed to stop stockpiling for the March Easter offensive.
